Title: Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/low-resource-programming-languages

Markdown Content:
Our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world. COBOL [supports⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/cobol) more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in [weather forecasting⁠(opens in a new window)](https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/71120) and [nuclear reactor safety analysis⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.nrc.gov/education-regulatory-research/research/computer-codes). Improving AI’s ability to work in these languages could help teams maintain and modernize the software that essential services depend on.

This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages. Maintaining and modernizing this software can be difficult: documentation may be incomplete, original developers may have left the company, and important business rules may only exist in code. Whether teams are fixing bugs or migrating to another language, they need to preserve the behavior their systems depend on.

To measure progress, we developed two evaluations. MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages. Our COBOL migration evaluation tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior. Together, they test two complementary skills: building new software and preserving what existing software does.

Our latest models show substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost.

On MultiLangBench, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across 20 programming languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, with improvements in every language tested. GPT‑6 Luna also outperforms GPT‑5.6 Sol, reaching 40.3% at approximately 78% lower estimated API cost.

On our COBOL migration evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with just 5.4% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while costing 39% less. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, nearly saturating the evaluation.

Together, these results show that our models are becoming significantly better at working with a wide range of programming languages, while also becoming more cost-efficient.

## 1. Building SQLite from scratch (MultiLangBench)

MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.

To compare implementations across languages, we use database files as a shared interface. The candidate program receives an initial database and a SQL query, then produces a modified database. We use the reference SQLite implementation to check whether the resulting database has the expected contents. This lets us apply the same tests regardless of the language used to build the engine.

We adapted tests from SQLite’s existing test suite to this format. The evaluation measures how much working functionality a model can build over an extended coding session, reporting both test pass rate and API cost.

At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across the 20 languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%). Astra scores above 83% in 19 of the 20 languages, with COBOL remaining the hardest at 72%.

GPT‑6 Luna offers a lower-cost option that also improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol in every language tested. At maximum reasoning effort, it reaches an average test pass rate of 40.3%. Gains include COBOL (10.9% to 17.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 34.1%), Fortran (21.4% to 31.4%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 41.6%). These improvements come at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT‑5.6 Sol, approximately 78% lower.

We are releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite on [GitHub⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/MultiLangBench), along with results for each language. Developers can inspect what the evaluation tests, review performance in the languages they use, and identify gaps that matter for their own work.

## 2. Migrating a COBOL codebase

Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.

Successful migration requires understanding both the program’s business logic and COBOL’s specific language behavior. COBOL programs often process financial transactions and business records, where details such as rounding rules and missing-record handling reflect business requirements. For example, COBOL’s fixed-point arithmetic discards excess decimal digits unless rounding is explicitly requested. A rewrite that rounds those values instead can run without errors while producing different financial results.

To test whether these behaviors are preserved, we evaluate our models on hidden tests that require byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs. A migration is considered successful only if all tests pass. Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.

On this evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT‑5.6 Sol’s 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation. These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on.

## Advancing capabilities for enterprise software

These evaluations, alongside direct feedback from developers and enterprise customers, help us see where our models are improving and where they still fall short.

Our goal is to help models apply software engineering skills across more languages: understanding unfamiliar repositories, planning changes, using build tools, running tests, and debugging failures.

You can try our latest models through the API on coding tasks in the languages your team uses. Your feedback on what works, where the models struggle, and which languages or workflows we should focus on next helps shape how we train and evaluate models to better support the software you depend on.

Title: Germany Wants to Lead the World in Industrial AI: How NVIDIA Will Help

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/germany-wants-to-lead-the-world-in-industrial-ai-how-nvidia-will-help/

Published Time: 2026-10-19T19:27:08+00:00

Markdown Content:
In the cavernous hall of Kraftwerk, a former power station in Berlin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang sat down to discuss Germany’s AI roadmap, and in particular, the industrial applications of AI.

Huang opened by tracing NVIDIA’s longstanding relationship with German industry, beginning with gaming systems, workstations and automotive design in the early 2000s and leading to today’s partnerships in autonomous vehicle development and digital twins for manufacturing.

The conversation focused on how Germany can make the most of the AI revolution by playing to its strengths in manufacturing and automotive — and by encouraging AI adoption across the country’s ecosystem of small and medium-sized companies.

Earlier in the day, as part of the Invest in Germany Summit, Chancellor Merz, the Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy and the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space signed a Joint Declaration of Intent with NVIDIA.

The German federal government’s aim is to merge traditional German engineering and manufacturing expertise with cutting-edge research and AI technology. The declaration sets out an agreement to work on a joint initiative with NVIDIA to advance cutting edge AI models for physical AI.

Formalizing and expanding NVIDIA’s collaboration with Germany’s federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” which is comprised of representatives from politics, industry, research and trade associations, helps achieve the government’s stated goal to “systematically bring industrial AI into widespread use and to establish a state-of-the-art industrial AI ecosystem in Europe.”

## **Germany’s Ambition to Integrate AI With Industry**

Merz and Huang dug into industrial AI and how NVIDIA can help Germany lead the way. The German Chancellor first laid out his government’s ambition.

“We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said. “I’m really optimistic that we will be one of the leading, if not the leading, country in the world in terms of the spread of AI for all the companies — our manufacturers, machinery, automotive industry and suppliers of the automotive industry. I think this is a great opportunity.”

Merz called out the leaders of the small and medium businesses — the Mittelstand — in the audience.

“The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”

Huang agreed, and praised Germany’s world-class expertise in manufacturing companies both large and small, as well as its math and science excellence. That national expertise and knowledge is what sets the German economy apart, he said, and AI will only amplify it.

“That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.”

Germany’s expertise with physical technologies is a differentiator, Huang and Merz agreed, and a powerful accelerator for the German economy when AI is included.

“If we are successful in bringing these two aspects and parts of the business of the future together,” Merz said. “I’m really very optimistic that Germany can be one of the most successful economies in the world.”

Huang described AI’s impact across virtually every industry as a new industrial revolution.

“This industrial revolution is so mighty, so powerful,” Huang said. “In the Chancellor’s words, you are re-engineering Germany. This is your chance to do it well.”

Merz envisioned a regular reunion with Huang to assess the progress Germany is making with AI.

“I would like to see him regularly, let’s say at least once a year, and discuss the progress we made,” Merz said, “And see a guy sitting in my office being extremely happy about Germany as a place to invest.”

## **NVIDIA’s Investments in Germany**

Huang also announced new investments in four German startups, part of a nearly $10 billion commitment by NVIDIA to support companies, universities, research institutions and more across Europe.

NVIDIA has been investing across Germany’s startup ecosystem, supporting leading technology companies including n8n, Neura Robotics and Black Forest Labs.

Today, Huang announced new planned investments in Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace.

Agile Robots, a Munich-based robotics company, builds AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare.

Avelios Medical, a Munich-based healthcare technology startup, develops an AI-native hospital information system that serves as the core system of record for clinical and administrative workflows, integrating AI directly into hospital operations to free up doctors and nurses to deliver better patient care.

Mirelo, a German startup, develops AI models that generate sound effects, speech and music for video, helping creators and production teams produce high-quality audio that perfectly matches their visuals on screen.

Reflex Aerospace, a Berlin-based space scaleup, designs and builds high-performance satellites ready for launch in about 12 months instead of years.

## **Siemens and NVIDIA Advance Autonomous Manufacturing; Record-Breaking Quantum Simulation**

Earlier in the day, Siemens announced it’s partnering with NVIDIA to advance AI-driven, autonomous factories. Siemens [showcased new AI solutions at its Erlangen factory](https://blogs.nvidia.com/gtc-berlin-2026-news/#entry-postlet-siemens-and-nvidia-put-industrial-ai-to-work-in-erlangen), advancing its role as a global blueprint for autonomous manufacturing. Fully virtual production ramp-up reduces engineering effort by up to 85%, while agent-based production planning enables more adaptive manufacturing and cost savings of up to 20%.

NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER, Europe’s largest supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, to run a [record-breaking simulation](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-runs-record-simulation-of-fault-tolerant-quantum-computing-at-julich-supercomputing-centre) of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The 104-qubit simulation is the largest and most detailed of its kind to date.

# NVIDIA Advances Agentic Security for Media, From European Public Service Broadcasting to Global Content Production

 Expanded sovereign standards with the EBU help European broadcasters protect editorial independence and cultural identity, while NVIDIA-accelerated Adobe Frame.io workflows help studios find content faster across massive content libraries.

October 19, 2026 by[Richard Kerris](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/author/rkerris/ "Posts by Richard Kerris")

 Share

Share This Article

At a creative industry event that took place today in Berlin — hosted in collaboration with Adobe, Bertelsmann, NVIDIA and UFA — the latest advancements in intelligent media were on display.

Key to the news: the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is collaborating with NVIDIA to expand its sovereign framework with cloud, open models and integration partners, while Adobe Frame.io is accelerating video agent search capabilities with NVIDIA GPUs, helping German TV and film producer UFA find the right moments faster.

Read more about both announcements below.

## **Sovereign Clouds and Open Models Built for European Broadcasters**

The EBU and NVIDIA are expanding the sovereign standards they [introduced](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/european-broadcasting-union-sovereign-ai/) last year for European public service media. The initiative now brings in sovereign cloud providers, open model developers and systems integrators to define how broadcasters can deploy agents while keeping control of their data, infrastructure, models and security.

The EBU is the world’s leading alliance of public service media, with over 115 member organizations in more than 55 countries reaching over 1 billion people. As agents move into newsrooms, production and audience services, those broadcasters need a foundation that protects editorial independence, data sovereignty and national resilience.

The expanded initiative is turning those principles into deployable services. It’ll define requirements and reference architectures for where workloads run, how data is governed, which models power services and how systems stay secure throughout their lifecycle.

“These standards give EBU members a shared foundation to strengthen resilience, retain control and deliver accountable advanced services that sustain audience trust,” said Annsofi Eriksson, chief technology officer at the EBU.

Cloud providers will map the standards to sovereign deployment options:

*   Microsoft will bring expertise from Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, including Azure Local and Foundry Local, so broadcasters can process sensitive editorial material locally and keep critical services running when external connectivity is down.
*   Nebius offers a platform for broadcasters to train, fine-tune and run their own models on European infrastructure.

Open models give broadcasters the visibility to inspect, evaluate and adapt AI for local languages, archives and editorial policies. [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open models provide a foundation broadcasters can customize for domain-specific applications and public-service requirements.

“Sovereign cloud infrastructure and open models can help Europe’s public service media innovate while protecting data, editorial independence and cultural diversity,” said Delphine Ernotte, CEO of France Télévisions and president of the EBU.

Media-specific consulting and systems integration provided from Qvest and other system integrators to ensure that reference architectures are practical, interoperable and deployable in real world broadcast environments.

## **Adobe****Frame.io Speeds Video Search With NVIDIA Accelerated Computing**

Also at the event, Adobe is highlighting its latest enhancements that help creatives search through video data faster.

Adobe is using NVIDIA accelerated computing to help creative teams find and work with video content faster. Its GPU-accelerated search pipeline uses [NVIDIA NVDEC](https://developer.nvidia.com/video-codec-sdk)for video decoding, [TensorRT](https://developer.nvidia.com/tensorrt) for optimized AI inference and the [CUDA platform](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-zone) for preprocessing and embedding generation.

Adobe is also advancing GPU-accelerated media ingest using NVIDIA NVENC and NVDEC to accelerate video encoding and decoding, helping production teams process growing media libraries more efficiently.

The results: about 5x faster embedding generation, up to 4x higher throughput and up to 5x lower latency for search processing. A new two-frame-per-second proxy, about 80% smaller than the 360p version it replaces, cuts storage and transfer while keeping the visual detail search needs.

That speed matters for UFA, one of Germany’s leading film and TV producers. It delivers more than 3,500 hours of programming a year, including the daily drama “Gute Zeiten, schlechte Zeiten.” When editors build a recap or flashback, they may need a specific reaction or unresolved exchange from as far back as 15 years — something file names and folders can’t surface.

Frame.io semantic search finds moments inside videos by concept, action or setting, and hybrid search adds notes, transcripts and approval status. An editor can search for “a character looking concerned,” narrow by character name and filter to approved footage, then move straight into review.

The work is part of a broader Adobe and NVIDIA collaboration that also spans Adobe Substance 3D, Firefly Foundry and 3D digital twin workflows for enterprises.

Nscale and Anthropic are reportedly in talks for yet another $45 billion compute deal
A little over a month ago, Anthropic and AI infrastructure provider Nscale
announced a $45 billion compute deal
. Now, the duo may be about to do it again.
Bloomberg
reports that
the two companies are said to be on the verge of announcing yet another $45 billion compute deal, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources cautioned that talks are still under way and that the details could change.
If the deal goes through, it would be the latest in a long string of giant compute deals Anthropic has struck
over the past year
. TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Anthropic for more information and will update this story if we hear back.
The massive amount of money being sunk into AI compute deals has

articles.content:
AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another.
However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future.
With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released?
“Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part [of that] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added.
Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the
stickier aspects of benchmarking
— and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry.
Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations.
“They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said.
“They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.”
The
idea of embedded evaluators
— in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with
a rash of safety incidents
that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face
was famously  the target
of one of those incidents.
Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s
decision to hire Accenture
as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some
critics mocking
the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand.
Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily out perform a frontier model, Soleiman shared.
“Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added.
In other words: the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary.

articles.content:
Microsoft on Monday
introduced new security features
designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes at Microsoft
continues to warn enterprises about the dangers
of AI and agents.
Perhaps the most notable addition is
Guardian Agents
, a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.
Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.
The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”
Earlier this month,
in his private blog
, Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.
“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”
When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.
“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”
On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.
Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.
The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.
Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”
Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.
This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.
Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which
garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies.
The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new
Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents
, which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.

articles.content:
On Monday, Amazon Web Services released a tool called
TorchNeuron
that lets AI startups easily move their AI apps onto Amazon’s AI chip, Trainium. In doing so, Amazon is also taking a direct stab at the software advantage that has helped Nvidia become the default hardware choice for AI apps and spurred its rise as AI hardware provider of choice.
TorchNeuron works with PyTorch, a free, open source toolkit that developers use to build, train, and run AI models. It lets AI apps written with PyTorch run on Trainium by changing just one line of configuration, according to Amazon — no code rewrite required.
Amazon says about 85% of AI apps are written with PyTorch. Facebook originally developed it, but since 2022, it has been part of the Linux Foundation, which maintains open source projects. Nvidia has spent years ensuring its CUDA software — the software infrastructure that allows apps to run on Nvidia GPUs and its other hardware — seamlessly supports AI apps written with PyTorch. As a result, Nvidia’s hardware is now deeply embedded in the toolkit, essentially by default.
TorchNeuron is adapted from PyTorch, so developers who know PyTorch already know how to use it. Amazon isn’t the first company to attempt to easily bring their chips to the platform. PyTorch users can also port their apps to AMD GPUs or even Apple’s chips with a simple configuration change.
However, Amazon argues that porting to Trainium is not only easy, but it also gives AI startups access to Amazon’s entire cloud. Unsurprisingly, AWS claims that this is a better choice for startups than using neoclouds, many of which are tied to Nvidia and its hardware, like CoreWeave, Nebius, and Firmus.
“You’re building on AWS. You’re not betting on a single-purpose compute provider and scrambling to build everything else around it,” Colin Brace, VP of Technology Software at AWS Annapurna Labs (the unit that makes Amazon’s custom chips), told TechCrunch via email. “On AWS,” he continued, “the infrastructure to go from prototype to production is already there, allowing a founder to move fast and scale when they need to.”
AWS says that because the same chip both handles training (teaching the AI model) and inference (putting the finished model to work, as when it answers a user’s question), and is tightly integrated with the cloud infrastructure that startups need, its cloud will save them money, even if AWS doesn’t offer the cheapest per-token price.
“Trainium’s value is price-performance plus the fact that it’s one platform for both training and inference, which improves the economics across a full workload,” Brace said. “Look at Deepgram — they
moved to Trainium
using native PyTorch support and they’re processing 70% more audio per dollar at production-grade accuracy.”
Deepgram
is an AI voice app provider, a competitor to ElevenLabs.
But Amazon isn’t content to just give PyTorch app developers an easy option to move to its cloud.
Amazon also says it is pushing PyTorch to be less automatically centered on Nvidia, and it will contribute the code to do that to the main PyTorch project. In the blog post announcing the new tool, the
company wrote
:
Amazon’s approach extends beyond its own hardware. The company is contributing changes upstream to PyTorch itself, working with the PyTorch community to remove code that ties the framework to specific chips. The goal is to make PyTorch more hardware-agnostic for the entire developer community, not just Trainium users.
While such a tactic is undoubtedly good for those who are selling hardware and cloud services that compete with Nvidia, one of the points of PyTorch is to hide all the pesky difficulties of getting AI code to run on hardware. We’ll have to wait and see if pushing Nvidia out that far gives developers more choice and more affordable options, as Amazon promises, or just more configuration headaches.
Either way, if Amazon succeeds in deeply uncoupling PyTorch from Nvidia, this could have much bigger ramifications for the GPU giant than simply dealing with chip competitors. As Brace said: “The real story is removing the lock-in that kept developers from having a real choice at all.”

articles.content:
OpenCode
, an open source AI coding agent that has been gaining ground among developers as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight, affecting 1.4% of users of its online platform, OpenCode Console, where some users store the API keys, or digital passwords, they use to access AI services.
As the OpenCode team struggled to keep pace with the attack, the scramble to respond highlighted a growing problem: Companies without vetted access to AI models with fewer safety restrictions have a hard time defending against large-scale, AI-driven cyberattacks.
“We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the company
wrote
on X. “We have notified them all this morning via email.” Users who did not receive an email were not impacted, the company said.
While the company didn’t specify how the distillation attack occurred, leaked API keys can help users in countries with restricted access to American models generate the high volume of outputs needed for that process. Some
skeptics
called the framing an overstretch, arguing that the incident was a straightforward breach whose use for distillation remains unproven.
Overnight, developers began posting spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X: “I saw my Open AI, Anthropic, and Google AI spend alerts all fire off before going to bed wondering what was going on,” a developer
wrote
.
Other users reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on individual accounts; a few described totals above $1,000.
Anthropic
and
Google
both blocked the API keys they believed were exposed, while
OpenAI
said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode said
refunds
for unauthorized charges are underway.
The exposed keys were confined to Console, where some users had them in workspaces. The open source app and command-line tool were not affected, according to co-founder Dax Raad. “Note this is the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself, those keys never come to us,” he
wrote
on X.
Even as users and AI companies moved to disable the exposed keys, the OpenCode team was still under pressure. Raad
said
attackers had been trying to break into its systems nonstop for 48 hours, requiring the team to keep AI defensive agents running around the clock. AI models that the OpenCode team turned to for analysis helped for a while, but started refusing to work when the malicious code they were asked to examine activated safety filters.
“[T]hat was a bit frustrating,” he wrote on X.
OpenCode later received access to OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users AI models that are less likely to refuse requests for defensive security work. Raad said the access improved the team’s ability to investigate the attack.
OpenCode isn’t the first company to hit this wall. In July, AI platform Hugging Face
said
commercial AI models blocked its attempts to analyze activity logs from an intrusion by autonomous AI agents, which OpenAI
later revealed
were its own models running with safeguards lowered during a test. In a section of its blog post titled “The asymmetry problem,” Hugging Face wrote that guardrails “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.”
Security researchers have
raised similar complaints
, saying the restrictions are inconsistent and have pushed some toward foreign open-weight models, which anyone can download and run.
The weekend episode drew a response from David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
“OpenCode (and earlier Hugging Face) hit the same wall mid-attack: frontier models refused to analyze the very exploits needed for defense because the payloads tripped safety filters. The guardrails backfired,” he
wrote on X
.
The breach occurred the same night OpenCode
made
GLM-5.3-Flash free for users. The broader GLM-5.3 family has
drawn
attention from researchers who study open-weight models and note that its cybersecurity capabilities approached levels previously associated with restricted-access models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview.
OpenCode has not detailed how attackers gained access to the older system, how keys were stored, or the full extent of any misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. The company said the incident
remains ongoing
.
The breach lands amid a run of AI-enabled cyber incidents. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike
said
a China-based hacker likely used an AI penetration-testing agent, which probes computer systems for weaknesses, and Claude in attacks on
South Korean banks
. Last week, India’s cybersecurity agency
warned
that AI agents, including some being tested by AI companies, had reached Indian organizations’ systems without authorization.

articles.content:
Tolan
, the AI companion designed to help people manage their daily lives, navigate relationships and emotions, and accomplish their goals, has just expanded its runway with another $30 million in capital.
The startup’s investors in the latest round include Union Square Ventures, Khosla Ventures, and Homebrew, doubling the total amount it has raised to date and pushing its valuation beyond the previous $120 million, according to a new report by
Upstarts Media
. (The startup didn’t disclose its new valuation, but
PitchBook
estimates it at more than $268 million, with “medium confidence.”)
Users engage with Tolan’s app through a cartoonish character that’s meant to offer support and help them get through their to-dos.
Image Credits:
Tolan on App Store
Tolan generates revenue from its tiered memberships, which are required for full access to all features. The company told Upstarts Media its annual recurring revenue is now in the “double-digit millions.”
The startup is one of the few AI companions that have found some traction, as it claims to have more than 250,000 active users who have had more than 70 million conversations over the past year. Around 70% of its users are women, and 40% are parents, Tolan’s team told the news outlet. (Anecdotally, the app is said to appeal in particular
to neurodivergent people
, who may benefit from additional support, whether that’s emotional support or help with organizing tasks.)
Compared with other companions, Tolan seems to have found a balance between being helpful without being perceived as too weird. Compare that with the public shaming that Friend’s pendant-based AI companion faced; users dubbed Friend “
very cringe
,”
The New York Times
called it “hated,” and
Wired
said it “has no soul.”
Meanwhile, another former top contender in the space, Character.AI, recently
filed for bankruptcy
after its
founder’s return to Google
. (Its remaining staff is transitioning to Disney, which bought some of its assets.)
However, Tolan could end up facing increased competition from the more recent crop of AI agents, which help users plan, organize, and accomplish their tasks and goals, not just talk their way through them. For instance, Meta gave its AI agent Muse a cute avatar for its users to talk to, which it also plans to
release as a hardware product in the future.
The startup also has to navigate the risks of offering AI-powered emotional support, given that
multiple
lawsuits
have been
filed against general-purpose AI app makers
alleging that chatbot interactions contributed to users’ suicides.

articles.content:
Twelve years ago today, Eugenia Kuyda stood up
onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt
and presented a conversational chatbot called IO that acted as a lifestyle concierge to help people book restaurants and vacations along with other tasks.
IO, the first product from her startup Luka, came before the deep learning breakthroughs that would eventually lead to today’s large language models. “
It still worked
,” Kuyda told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It was pretty magical … but, of course, it’s nowhere near what we have today.”
Luka ended up becoming Replika, the popular AI chatbot companion company. Last year, Kuyda left as CEO of Replika and founded
Wabi
.
The technology has finally caught up with her original vision for Luka, just in time for Wabi to take on a wave of new personal AI assistants such as
Muse
and
Instinct
, which promise to do everything from manage your inbox to find you the best flight deals.
our launch video from 2015 – Luka later pivoted into
@replika
. we were building personal agents 11 years ago!
https://t.co/OBQqCF1MeW
pic.twitter.com/rIS3ljEZFq
— Eugenia Kuyda (@ekuyda)
October 7, 2026
On Monday, Kuyda officially launched Wabi for all users, a multiplayer personal AI assistant that functions as a messenger app, allowing users to maintain multiple agentic threads dedicated to different tasks and long-term goals. Within each thread, users can build and use custom apps, like a weight-loss tracker inside a health thread or an app showing nearby children’s events inside a family thread.
The launch is something of a
pivot for Wabi
, though Kuyda describes it as more of an evolution. When
TechCrunch covered Wabi’s initial launch
last year, along with its $20 million pre-seed round, it was described as more of a social platform where you could create mini apps with prompts that you could share with friends or across the app.
Over the past year, Kuyda said the team realized that while people love personal software rather than “one size fits all solutions in the App Store,” they “maybe don’t want to spend a lot of time, or any time, building it.”
With Wabi 2.0, the agent decides what apps to build. The moment you connect it to your email, it automatically spins up a number of threads and apps to start with, and users can add to that by requesting custom apps or starting new threads.
“It’s doing what Instinct and Muse do, but it also has all these apps, which helps users do more stuff,” Kuyda said.
App-building isn’t Wabi’s only differentiator. Kuyda is also betting on its multithreaded, multiplayer design.
“It’s not just everything in one single thread like with Instinct and Muse, where you get buried in the information that it sends you every day,” Kuyda said. “Single thread experiences, if you think about it, get worse over time because it’s just so much context in one endless conversation.”
The longer an AI chatbot conversation goes on, the more likely it is to hallucinate, lose track of context, or respond in ways that would otherwise be blocked by safety guardrails, according to interviews with AI researchers.
Image Credits:
Wabi
Threads can also be shared, functioning as group chats.
“Today, all the agentic apps are just [conversations] between you and the agent, and I feel like it should be a lot more about bringing people together in a group chat together,” Kuyda said. “Not you doing it separately with your AI, and I’m doing it separately with my AI … I don’t think anyone has yet cracked multiplayer.”
Kuyda walked TechCrunch through some of her own shared threads. In one with her boyfriend, a row of apps along the top helps the two of them connect and find things to do together, including a live music tracker, an app that asks a question every day about their relationship, a running list of restaurant suggestions, important events from their shared calendar, and a list of books they’re reading together with suggestions for what to read next.
In her more family-focused thread, there is an app tracking her daughter’s schedule, another for finding kid-friendly events nearby, and another that quizzes her daughter on Japanese.
Within any shared chat, users can share as much or as little as they want, from email and calendar information to bank account details.
“So my partner can ask Wabi in the chat, ‘Is Eugenia free next Thursday?’ or ‘Did she buy those tickets?’” Kuyda said. She noted that access is scoped to individual chats, and everyone in a chat can see when someone’s personal information is requested.
On privacy more broadly, Wabi is SOC 2 compliant, meaning its data security controls have been independently audited. Wabi runs entirely in the cloud, and most user data is stored in the U.S., Kuyda said.
“My previous company Replika worked on AI that will make people feel … less lonely,” Kuyda said. “To a degree, that is [in Wabi] as well. AI can bring people together, even when it comes to just helping you spend time better together in real life, whether it’s going out and seeing a concert together or finding the next book that you will read together.”
Wabi is free for now, and the company hasn’t settled on a business model yet. Kuyda said Wabi is in talks to raise more funds.

Tenstorrent hits $6.2B valuation to scale open-weight AI chips
Tenstorrent, a chip startup focused on inference, has raised $1.5 billion at a $6.2 billion valuation. The round comes five months after the 10-year-old Nvidia challenger
reportedly
received acquisition interest from Intel and Qualcomm at valuations of as much as $5 billion.
The fresh round, which more than doubled Tenstorrent’s valuation from the
$2.6 billion
it fetched in late 2024, was led by Trace Capital, a new firm launched by Quiet Capital co-founder Ben Mahdavi, and Innovation X. Other backers included Cadence Ventures, Eclipse, Fidelity, SanDisk, and T. Rowe Price.
Jim Keller, a prominent microprocessor engineer and Tenstorrent CEO, told Bloomberg that the company decided to remain independent and raise more capital after it showed that its Galaxy servers could run DeepSeek models. The new capital will go toward scaling chips tailored for serving open-weight AI models and video generation.
Tenstorrent is part of a wave of AI hardware startups trying to chip away at Nvidia’s dominance. Among them is Etched, an AI chip maker that was fielding investment offers at valuations of $40 billion or more,
TechCrunch reported
earlier this month.

articles.content:
The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for “vibe-coding” your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more.
One such solution, called “dumbtv,” describes its mission on its
GitHub page
thus: “Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for.”
Another, “
cleanyourtv
,” promises to strip the bloatware from any Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi, to replace the launcher with one that resembles Apple TV.
While hacking consumer electronics devices to gain more control over their systems is hardly a new idea, the latest advances in AI technology have made such efforts much more accessible to anyone. With smart TVs in particular, the hacks come at a time when people have grown frustrated with being forced to watch ads and put up with their devices surveilling their viewing habits.
Modern smart TVs ship with a technology called automatic content recognition (ACR), which identifies what’s playing on the screen using screenshots, audio clips, or other forms of digital fingerprinting.
If these “dumb TV” hacks become more popular among everyday consumers, they have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which profits from selling viewing data to advertisers or using it to display personalized ads on their own interfaces.
As the creator of cleanyourtv, Gathin T., puts it, the idea to clean up the smart TV interface started one afternoon when he got tired of seeing the ads on his parents’ TV set.
Vibe coded my parents' TV this afternoon!
It was showing a sponsored ad before you could even get to Netflix.
Gave Claude Code the model number, it found the TV on wifi, removed 25 Xiaomi packages and wrote a new launcher.
Looks like an Apple TV now lol
pic.twitter.com/E5Q4A1b0yI
— Gathin (Ø,G) (@gathint)
October 17, 2026
“I had Claude Code clean it up over Wi-Fi and build a simple home screen with just their apps on it. I put the prompt on GitHub, tweeted the before and after, and a few thousand people did the same to their own TVs over the next two days. Xiaomi, TCL, Sony, Fire TV, LG, a projector or two,” the developer wrote on a
website
for donations, linked from the project’s
homepage
.
The solution doesn’t require gaining root access to the TV, nor does it make it impossible to return to the factory default state, if desired.
Meanwhile, the dumbtv solution has been tested end-to-end on a Fire TV Edition television set and Android/Google TV platforms on TVs from Sony, TCL, Philips, Hisense, Xiaomi, and Shield. To use this hack, the developer, Muzzammil Yasin Sabuwala,
suggests
pointing your preferred AI agent at the dumbtv repository on GitHub.
Sabuwala said he was motivated to work on dumbtv because he was tired of the ads and not being able to delve directly into the content he wanted to watch. His solution was coded using a combination of Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, he told TechCrunch, and he plans to maintain the GitHub, adding support for more models over time.
introducing dumbtv
– no spying
– no ads from tv
– fully customisable
to setup just point your agent to this repo –
https://t.co/prQLD17Wa4
https://t.co/z41SWJZVXt
pic.twitter.com/c6R8EhljiA
— Muzzammil (@DevMuzzammil)
October 18, 2026
Fair warning: All these solutions are works in progress, and various users are now testing them across different TV platforms and suggesting updates and fixes.
However, individuals don’t need to borrow someone else’s work from GitHub to get the job done.
In
one newly viral X post, Ryan Doyle
explains that he simply sent Claude Code the listing for his TV and asked “Can you hack this?” The agent then talked him through the process, allowing him to remove the ads and bloatware from the TV set, speed up the lagging user interface, and customize his screensaver, he claims.
Doyle then goes on to demonstrate in a video how fast and responsive the new interface is after the AI made the requested changes.
This is how fast the TV moves now that Claude deleted all the BS laggy bloatware it comes with
https://t.co/nUCEjqPwAO
pic.twitter.com/g07CEgC1GJ
— Ryan Doyle (@doooyle)
October 17, 2026
Seeing posts about people “vibe-coding their TVs,” inspired one X user, Mihir Gupta, to try it himself.
“One afternoon with Claude Code: 25 bloat apps disabled, the 192 MB stock launcher replaced with a custom 83 MB one, plus rotating wallpapers,” he
wrote
.
The end result of these hacks may be mixed, however.
Some people have found
that Claude
wouldn’t respond
to their simple
suggestions
to “hack my TV,” necessitating more complex prompts. Others warned that AI agents could make mistakes, possibly disabling important packages or breaking things in the process. One person even said they
bricked their Android TV using Claude
, and
another got stuck halfway through
hacking their Fire TV.
For those wary of using AI to fully hack their TVs, there are existing solutions for customizing Android-based smart TVs, such as home screen replacement apps ATV Launcher, Projectivy Launcher, and FLauncher.

articles.content:
Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing.
The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise. While it uses fewer parameters than the
Nemotron 3 Ultra
model, Nvidia says it can deliver similar accuracy in instruction-following and tool-use tasks.
At the other end of the spectrum, the company also launched two lightweight Bolt models. These are intended to run locally on the new AI PCs (running the Nvidia RTX Spark chip) and workstations running the DGX Spark. Such PCs, aimed at consumers, programmers, and enterprise knowledge workers, are being
released right now into the market through partners like Microsoft and Dell.
“Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski,
wrote in the blog post
announcing these models.
Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks. These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience.
While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL. These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity, and
Salesforce
.
Of course, these aren’t the first open-weight models that Nvidia has released that compete with the proprietary frontier labs — companies that are both its customers and its investments. The GPU giant has an entire family of
Nemotron
models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation.
However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips.
So Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers. “Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and own what they build,” Briski wrote.
But with the announcement or the smaller, local PC models, it is also trying to push forward the nascent trend of consumer AI assistants. While it seems a new AI assistant is introduced every day by startups and Big Tech alike, privacy-weary consumers may not want to invite such agents so deeply into their lives giving them access to info about their families, health, finances, and so on.
So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote.
Of the two Bolt models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74-billion parameter model designed for local agentic tasks. It is intended to balance speed with reasoning to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing. The smallest Bolt E4B is aimed at conversational agents.
Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

articles.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
articles.title_ko: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
articles.summary: University of Michigan spinout Laplace Intelligence uses AI agents and interactive simulation to stress-test robots and self-driving vehicles before deployment. The profitable startup is competing in Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt, October 13-15 in San Francisco.
articles.summary_ko: , told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.” Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it. “Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
articles.content:
If there’s one lesson the
OpenAI-Hugging Face incident
taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable.
“Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of
Laplace Intelligence
, told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.”
Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it.
“Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said.
Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at
TechCrunch Disrupt
in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will
present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon
, October 13.
Howie Sun, CEO, Laplace Intelligence.
Image Credits:
Laplace Intelligence
Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a
paper
on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas.
“I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said.
Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision.
“We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said.
At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity
simulation
reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world.
The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale.
Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom.
Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision.
“It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.”
While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop.
“They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said.
Henry Liu, chief scientist, Laplace Intelligence.
Image Credits:
Laplace Intelligence
Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training —
self-driving truck company Waabi
comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world.
“There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.”
Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto and a major Japanese automotive manufacturer.
Laplace is also working with Nvidia and T-Mobile on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses.
Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals.
Chief among its rivals is
Applied Intuition
, a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation.
Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.”
“That will be the biggest moat,” he said.

Justine Calma
is a senior science reporter covering energy and the environment with more than a decade of experience. She is also the host of
Hell or High Water: When Disaster Hits Home
, a podcast from Vox Media and Audible Originals.
The US is building more fossil fuel infrastructure than it has in a decade while renewable energy growth slows down, a new
report
shows.
Electricity demand is also climbing faster than it has in
more than a decade
with more data centers, factories, and electric vehicles plugging into the grid. Despite those growing demands, the Trump administration has
sought to hobble
the wind and solar industries in favor of fossil fuels.
America’s energy landscape is already shifting as a result, according to the report published last week by the nonprofit Environmental Defense Fund and research firm Atlas Public Policy. If all the gas projects in the development pipeline complete construction, they could lock in more pollution and higher electricity prices for decades, the authors warn.
“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point”
“The U.S. power sector is at a new inflection point, with decisions made today shaping the cost, reliability, and emissions profile of the grid for decades to come,” the report says.
While the US still generates
60 percent of its electricity from fossil fuels
, renewables have quickly gained ground. Wind and solar produced more electricity together than coal
for the first time in 2024
. Solar was the fastest-growing source of new electricity generation that year, accounting for 81 percent of added capacity. Globally, solar has become the
cheapest
power source
in most of the world.
Then Donald Trump stepped into his second term as president with a plan to “drill, baby, drill” for fossil fuels, his
preferred power source for energy-hungry data centers
. His administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects by
issuing stop work orders
,
blocking
permits
, and
removing
tax incentives
. We’re still seeing a rush of
new solar and wind farms
driven by relatively low costs, although many of them make up the last wave of projects that benefited from Biden-era incentives.
The winds are shifting in favor of gas-fired power plants. Plans for new fossil fuel infrastructure climbed from just 5 percent of all new capacity in 2024 to 30 percent by the second quarter of 2026, according to the new report, which analyzes data from the US Energy Information Administration. If the trend continues, fossil fuels could make up 70 percent of the development pipeline by the end of the decade. Planned fossil capacity would reach 68 gigawatts by 2030, reflecting a 45 percent jump from construction plans just six months ago.
Many of those plans could still fall through, particularly if forecasts for AI data center energy demand are overblown. But for now, renewable energy projects are being canceled at a faster clip than fossil fuels, at 4.9 percent compared to 2.9 percent of projects, respectively.
New utility-scale solar and wind farms still beat gas when it comes to cost, coming in at $68 to $69 per megawatt-hour on average compared to $90 per megawatt-hour for new combined-cycle natural gas plants, the report finds. Fossil fuels are also subject to increasing
price volatility
, particularly since the US instigated war with Iran. Gas and coal power plants also emit air pollutants and the greenhouse gases causing climate change, leading to more health costs. Electricity
bills have
risen
across the nation as utilities upgrade power grids and build new energy infrastructure to meet rising demand.

CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
by
Elizabeth Lopatto
Oct 19, 2026, 9:28 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift

Elizabeth Lopatto
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.
CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into
distressed territory
by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath
“SPAC King”
Palihapitiya
noticed the distressed debt
, and also
asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble
. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.
Now, I have
also
asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “
How are we planning on affording this, champs?
”, that’s a very different signal. When
I say “yikes,”
it’s one thing. When
Elon Musk says it
, that’s something else.
When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more
To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders,
told the
Financial Times
—
also
last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.
“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,”
Bloomberg
quoted John Yovanovic
, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.
I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.
CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of
its second quarter earnings
, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it
pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans
, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.
The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds
So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.
Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize,
CoreWeave is probably fine for a while
. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.
Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been
a sell-off in Oracle bonds
, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.
Anyway,
some people are buying the dip
.

Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to
findings from the AI security firm Norforge
. Though Norforge doesn’t name the targets,
Reuters
reports
that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins.
Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches
have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time,
rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks
of their own after escaping from testing environments.
Researchers at Norforge uncovered the attacks through exposed work on Cairn, an open-source AI platform that
describes itself
as a “general-purpose problem-solving engine.” With Cairn, users set a start and end point for the AI agents, which document their progress as they move forward with the task. However, as noted by Norforge, hackers can also use the tool to orchestrate cyberattacks using AI agents.
The hacker who broke into more than 100 sites was the “most active” among the exposed Cairn instances discovered by Norforge, waging attacks on companies based in the US, Canada, Australia, and Japan, as reported by
Reuters
. This attacker laid out “preferred intrusion tactics” using fewer than 100 Chinese characters, with successful breaches taking about 23 hours, according to
Reuters
. Overall, Norforge found more than 20 exposed Cairn instances that are “likely malicious.”
In a statement to
The Verge
, Cummins spokesperson Melinda Koski said the company “is investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors.” A John Deere spokesperson told
Reuters
that there’s “no indication that ​sensitive information was accessed” as a result of the attack, while SharkNinja said the breach impacted a standalone site with product support information, and that it has contained the threat.
John Deere and SharkNinja didn’t immediately respond to
The Verge
’s request for comment.
Related
AI is supercharging hacking, and your local hospitals and banks aren’t ready
Attack of the killer script kiddies
Norforge says it’s working to get the malicious Cairn instances taken down. Cairn’s creator, who goes by @le1xia0,
said earlier this month
that the platform “was never a ‘hacking tool,’” adding that “misuse is a human decision, not a feature of the engine.”

Added a statement from Cummins.
