Democrats think cracking down on AI could give them an edge
At a moment when voters are fearful of AI, Democrats are finding their footing.
by
Lauren Feiner
Oct 19, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Cath Virginia / The Verge | Photo by Stephen Morton, Getty Images
Lauren Feiner
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.
Democrats could win back control of Congress this November, and if they do, they’ll need to decide how to approach one of the country’s newest and thorniest political issues: AI.
Polls predict Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, which would put committee leadership back in their hands. That could usher in a wave of newfound scrutiny for AI companies. Top Democrats on key committees have already signaled their willingness to press the industry on
tax credits tied to data centers
and
recent hacking incidents
, and would be able to set committee agendas if they take over, allowing them to call CEOs to testify in Congress and demand documents that explain companies’ inner workings.
AI issues are already taking a leading role in campaign ads, particularly as data center development has driven residents across the political spectrum to packed local meetings. While President Donald Trump has opposed most regulation of the technology in favor of an accelerationist approach, public
opinion polling
has shown
that Americans have widespread concerns about how AI will impact jobs, education, and other aspects of life. The direction and intensity of that oversight, though, is up for grabs.
The issue of AI is “a hundred percent ready for the taking,” says Jesse Lehrich, a Democratic strategist who previously ran a tech accountability advocacy group and worked for Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign. “The question remains open as to whether Democrats are willing and able to seize that opportunity.” AI issues currently include a lot of different things, from monitoring and restricting the development of frontier models to dealing with the effects of job displacement or data centers’ energy demands. Across both parties, lawmakers are still figuring out where to put their stakes in the ground, and
early congressional proposals
have yet to gain broad consensus.
“The question remains open as to whether Democrats are willing and able to seize that opportunity”
AI caught many lawmakers off guard, says Rob Flaherty, former deputy campaign manager for Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign and a Biden White House alum who cohosts a podcast with Lehrich. “For a long time, Democrats were afraid to talk about it, either for a mix of not understanding it, or being afraid of the money that was going to be poured in by the AI industry,” Flaherty says. But as AI becomes more salient for voters, “there will be immense profit to whoever can speak to the world that we’re moving into at a volume that voters can hear and can feel.”
Flaherty
recently launched
a super PAC called Tomorrow Together with Karthik Ganapathy, a former state communications director for Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaign. The group launched its first
$4 million ad blitz
last week in battleground House races, attacking Republican candidates as out of touch on AI and referencing issues like kids’ online safety and data centers. The group is looking beyond the midterms toward the 2028 presidential election, aiming to hone Democrats’ messaging to double down on what resonates most with voters.
While data centers have been the most visible AI issue in many communities, Flaherty says his group’s polling found sweeping bans on state AI regulation — repeatedly pushed by Trump and congressional Republicans — are even more broadly unpopular. Democratic donor and venture capitalist Ron Conway
now regrets funding
Marc Andreessen-backed pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future, Jay Carney, a former Obama press secretary who now runs communications for Conway’s VC fund, told
Politico
.
As of June, LTF spent nearly $45 million over almost a year, with $31 million left in the pot
according to Federal Election Commission filing
s. “At a certain point, voters speak louder than money,” Flaherty says. Even governors who lean toward the center of the Democratic Party, like California’s Gavin Newsom or Pennsylvania’s Josh Shapiro, have taken bolder stances against AI in recent weeks. Newsom
issued an executive order
looking to create an AI “kill switch” after
previously vetoing a bill
that would have instituted some similar measures, and Shapiro
reversed course against data centers
.
Democrats are well positioned to capitalize on the negative sentiment toward AI
Democrats are well positioned to capitalize on the negative sentiment toward AI because Trump’s largely anti-regulation stance has boxed in his party. Though some Republicans, including Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), have carved out a more skeptical approach to AI, Lehrich says, “I cannot think of a bigger political gift than Donald Trump just wholly bear-hugging the industry and declaring that we must let data reign and any community that rejects data centers is backwards and poor.”
A more sweeping AI regulatory agenda might include embedding independent researchers into frontier labs, requiring more safety checks up front, and imposing more liability on tech companies for anything from how their tools affect kids to whether they’re used to discriminate against workers or housing applicants. Lawmakers could also consider ways to meet demands from constituents that AI companies help pay for job displacement and other impacts they’ll have on people’s lives.
“I cannot think of a bigger political gift than Donald Trump just wholly bear-hugging the industry”
AI is
still not the top issue driving voters
to the polls, but Flaherty says that’s not necessarily the right way to think about it. “AI is not an issue as much as it is a story,” he says. “It’s a story of politicians getting bought off by industry. It’s a story of a bunch of guys making you foot the bill for them getting rich while they’re coming to make your life worse. It is a story that fits the national vibe.”
Where exactly different policy lines should be drawn on AI is still somewhat unsettled. But Flaherty warns that Democrats risk giving up ground if they fail to take big enough swings. Voters are “giving politicians a lot of leeway to take big swings and to really reimagine stuff,” he says. If politicians only stick to basics like plans to retrain workers at community colleges, “I think we’re going to miss the bigness and the ingenuity that the moment calls for.”

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,
sign up here
.
Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots.
But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic
tripled
from August to September.
The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us.
Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would.
Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely.
TechCrunch
recently
reported
people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has
blocked
Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an
appeal
in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots.
These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently
wrote
on LinkedIn.
If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the
vast majority
of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already
welcoming the agents
by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans.
The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left.
How might this go? Perhaps websites become increasingly neglected as destinations for real people. Humans who want to browse and compare products themselves encounter worse interfaces. Verification systems are imperfect; imagine constantly being asked to verify that you’re a human, not an agent (and hey, maybe you’ll need to get your
iris scanned
to do so). That sweater you want doesn’t have one price listed for everyone but instead displays different prices to different people’s agents. You can never tell when your agent’s recommendation is influenced by advertisements or platform commissions.
That’s a far cry from the future promised by
Google
,
Anthropic
, and
OpenAI
, in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage. But that promise is not outlandish. Agents are capable of
genuinely helping people
by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example.
Whether they can
actually
be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do.
These rules are still being written. Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing. It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.

articles.content:
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a
26,000-word blog post
that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.
Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal.
After a summer filled with
revelations
that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a
better handle on the technology
it has built.
That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher
posted on X
: “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another
called it
“the most important AI paper of the year.”
Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.”
I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.”
“I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.”
Knotted networks
It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge.
Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. (
MIT Technology Review
chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as
one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025
.)
Back in 2020, Cammarata and his colleagues were
studying a small image-recognition model
called Inception v1. When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats.
The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Looking at other models appeared to back this up. The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot.
Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on
ways to untangle that knot
. But despite a
few breakthroughs
, progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to
understand an LLM in fine-grained detail
.
Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says. But then he took the trouble to really look.
Nothing but neurons
At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks. He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don't know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says.
What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don't want to give up too quickly.”
Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith. Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias. When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’”
But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.”
Back to cars and cats
Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says. But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around. Take the car-and-cat neuron. Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common.
It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says. “But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently. It probably took me five seconds.”
It turns out that the image-recognition model was packing cars and cats into the same place because pictures of both those things often feature a prominent shape that looks like a V: the face of a cat; the front of a car seen from the side.
Cammarata ran a few experiments to check what other things the neuron responded to and found they included the corner of a pool table, the pointed nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water into the air from its deck. He also checked what turned the neuron off and found that it included images with a round O shape, a kind of anti-V.
The model had stored cats and cars in the same place because at some level they look the same, says Cammarata. “And I was like, ‘Whoa, okay, I think I might just be misunderstanding neural networks in general.’”
Cammarata is not saying that he yet fully gets how LLMs (or any models) work. He is saying that he no longer thinks full understanding is impossible. “I previously thought there would be some really hard problems to solve,” he says.
“I now feel like if I had 100,000 years to go look through a frontier language model just one circuit at a time, there’s, like, a pretty good shot I would come up with a good understanding.”
He adds: “And if that's true, things are really good, because you’re about to get insanely smart agents at a ridiculous scale. And what would have taken me, you know, 100,000 years, we will be able to do much faster. Automated scientists are getting really good.”
Boundless optimism
Built by Google in 2014, Inception v1 is a far simpler model than anything at the cutting edge today. Cammarata and his colleagues have started looking at modern LLMs and plan to publish the technical results of that work soon. A lot of researchers are looking forward to seeing those details. “I appreciate that he looked at thousands of examples, but even a large number here is not a substitute for rigorous evaluation,” says Stanford University’s Potts.
In the meantime, some are pushing back hard on the hype. Jacob Hilton at the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit research lab based in Berkeley, who has collaborated with Cammarata in the past, doesn’t think his claims are as important as people are making out.
In a
series of posts on X
, Hilton notes that researchers understand less than 0.01% of the inner workings of top-tier LLMs. “I always appreciate Nick [Cammarata]’s boundless optimism when we hang out, but unfortunately this is giving the public an unrealistic picture of the state of the field,” he wrote. “For a full understanding, we need to go beyond neurons, and explain how they connect together to form circuits. How is this going? If we are aiming for a full understanding, things are not looking good!”
Neel Nanda at Google DeepMind, who helped pioneer mechanistic interpretability alongside Cammarata, is also skeptical. “This is interesting work, but I don’t think it’s a significant update to the big picture of interpretability,” he
wrote on X
.
Nanda agrees that understanding what individual neurons do could help researchers figure out why specific models misbehave. But like Hilton, he notes that neurons are just one piece of a far larger puzzle. “I do not agree with some people’s grander inferences like that this is substantial progress towards ambitious reverse engineering [or] solving interpretability,” he wrote.
Cammarata admits that a lot of people have taken what he said too far: “It’s not infinitely good news; it’s not everything solved,” he says. “There’s a bunch of open questions around, like how much the combinations of neurons matter versus just one at a time.”
Cammarata says his blog post landed at a time when people are looking for hope. In particular, he thinks the AI safety community—the researchers and policymakers most worried that powerful models will bring huge risks—needs a lifeline right now. They think that things are looking bad and that even if things do turn out okay, it will be because we got lucky, not because we fixed anything, he says: “I don’t really hear a lot of optimism.”
That’s why Cammarata thinks what he has to say matters. The job of figuring out how this technology works, and thus how to control it, has barely begun. But at least it’s not a nonstarter. “I think our job is to sort of try to think like the neural network,” he says. “My guess is that things will turn out pretty well, because it was in some sense designed to be read.”

	Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
	246 points by rzk 8 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 389 comments

I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me:

> I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I'm writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we're going to spend our time checking each line of code, it's going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you've built where you don't truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I'm used to understanding what I'm building. Now I'm trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I'm comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too?

How are you handling this?

 help

bitwizeshift 4 hours ago | next [–]

I’m surprised I haven’t see anyone say this yet, but I don’t let the LLM design the code at all, I let it implement a design I have created.

By that I mean that, rather than let the LLM do the entire structure, I take the time to create the full hierarchy of abstractions and actors that I want my code to do. I decide, at the UML level, how abstractions will sit and interact — and then I make the LLM implement those gaps.

The key thing here is that, by doing this, I DO know how the code works. I may not know how each unit is implemented, but I know each unit’s responsibilities and how they interact with one another. I’ve found that LLMs are HORRIBLE at writing decent abstractions, regardless of how much prompting and skills I’ve given it. It will always get the job done, but it will often be unmaintainable and require bigger and heavier refactors as I introduce more and more requirement changes.

But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out.

It takes a few hours up front to plan ahead, but it makes the LLMs job easier and use less tokens, and it makes the code better long term. I don’t care if one unit is suboptimal, as long as the abstraction is right — because at worst I can change an implementation for a better one later.

Title: Diffusion at Scale: Introducing Mercury 3 – Inception

URL Source: https://www.inceptionlabs.ai/blog/introducing-mercury-3

Markdown Content:
Today we’re introducing Mercury 3, the most capable diffusion-based LLM released to date. Across a range of benchmarks, Mercury 3 outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, while running 4–8x faster at 1,000+ tokens per second.

Mercury 3 demonstrates that text diffusion scales. It’s more than 40x larger than Mercury 1 and is vastly more intelligent, but just as fast.

Early-access partners already use Mercury 3 for voice and chat support, real-time tutoring, data engineering, and web navigation:

## Mercury 3 at a glance

*   **Quality:** On par or better than frontier speed-optimized models like GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5.

*   **Speed:** 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs.

*   **Context:** 1M tokens, up from 260K for Mercury 2.5

*   **Price:** $0.20 per million input and $0.70 per million output tokens.

    *   At launch, Mercury 3 is 50% off at $0.10 per 1M input and $0.35 per 1M output. Cached tokens are 90% off the input price.

## Diffusion at scale

When we launched Mercury 1, it was the first proof point that diffusion LLMs could be built for commercial applications. The open question in the AI community was whether diffusion LLMs could scale to compete with autoregressive models on complex use cases.

Mercury 3 answers that question: they can. We’ve scaled Mercury more than 40x in total parameters, and intelligence across a range of standard benchmarks has risen 3x from Mercury 1 (mini) to Mercury 3. The scaling laws that drove progress in autoregressive models hold for diffusion too.

## Mercury 3 in production

Early-access partners are already running Mercury 3 to power latency-sensitive applications such as browser use agents, interactive education, real-time search agents, and customer support.

### Browser Use Agents

Agents wait on the model at every step, so small delays compound quickly. Mercury keeps each pass fast, whether the agent is navigating websites, researching across sources, or analyzing logs and tracing incidents. Agents finish sooner and have time to try more approaches before answering.

We ran Mercury 3 inside our production web-agent harness against frontier models, on 50 live Mind2Web navigation tasks. Mercury 3 completed 50% of them, significantly more than GPT-6.1-Sol. It did so using the same token volume and the same number of agent steps as a frontier model, at a fraction of the per-token cost.

Shuhao Zhang, Cofounder, TinyFish AI

### Interactive Education

Learning runs on fast feedback loops, and any delay pulls a student out of the material. Mercury reasons through each request and responds in near real time, whether it’s a voice tutor carrying a conversation, an assistant grading work, or an app adapting the next question to what the student just got wrong.

Mercury 3 allowed us to give every student instant feedback without giving up reasoning. Hints, marked answers and definitions now come back in about a second, with quality as good as or better than the models we ran before. When a student is stuck on a question, that speed keeps them working instead of waiting, and it was a drop-in swap for our existing stack.

Michael Tong, Co-founder/CTO, General Learning aka RevisionDojo

### Real-time search agents

Search applications start to feel unresponsive after just a few seconds delay. Mercury 3 runs fast enough to process dozens of documents and still answer while the user is engaged.

On smart glasses, an answer that takes five seconds feels broken. In our Sense API tests, Octen search took about 80ms; model generation was the bottleneck. Mercury 3 delivered the best balance of speed and quality among the fast models we tested, with a median generation time of 0.9 seconds and a median end-to-end response time of 2.2 seconds.

Kuan Zou, Founder & CEO, Octen AI

### Customer support

Support agents have to answer quickly, often for regulated businesses where a wrong answer is costly. Mercury keeps responses conversational without sacrificing accuracy.

At Lorikeet, we help complex and regulated businesses build a concierge for their customers that works across voice, chat and email. In chat and voice, customers need fast responses, but we can't compromise on accuracy or getting the job done correctly. In early testing, Mercury 3 beat other models on latency while also performing higher on evals and in production.

Michael Gribben, Member of Technical Staff, Lorikeet

## A real-time product portfolio

Mercury 3 is the flagship model in a widening portfolio of products that enable real-time AI.

*   **Mercury Voice:** Mercury Voice is customized for the extreme low-latency requirements of voice applications and for minimizing time to first answer token (TTFAT), not just end-to-end latency. It’s already powering agents at Audivi AI, Altur, and OpenCall.

*   **Mercury Decide:** Mercury Decide is a decision model built for high-volume classification. It outperforms Jev on benchmarks including JevBench and LegalBench.

## Get started

Mercury 3 is available today on the Inception API Platform and through OpenRouter, Baseten, and Vercel. It is OpenAI API compatible, so it drops into your existing stack with no rewrites. Enterprise deployments support dedicated capacity, autoscaling, compliance controls, and configurable data retention.

*   [**Try the API**](https://platform.inceptionlabs.ai/) with 100 million free tokens

*   **Enterprise evaluations:** we'll partner with you on workload fit, eval design, and performance under your serving constraints. [**Contact us**.](https://www.inceptionlabs.ai/enterprise#contact-sales)

## Mercury 3 is live. Diffusion scales.

[Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029) 45 points by [skull8888888](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=skull8888888)[8 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029) | [hide](https://news.ycombinator.com/hide?id=50154029&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154029) | [past](https://hn.algolia.com/?query=Launch%20HN%3A%20Laminar%20%28YC%20S24%29%20%E2%80%93%20RL-trained%20model%20that%20finds%20errors%20in%20agent%20traces&type=story&dateRange=all&sort=byDate&storyText=false&prefix&page=0) | [favorite](https://news.ycombinator.com/fave?id=50154029) | [22 comments](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029) Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar ([https://laminar.sh](https://laminar.sh/)). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark ([https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1](https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1)), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling. Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: [https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ](https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ) We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: [https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action](https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action) Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles. Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough. Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from. Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things. So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run. flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full. The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events. Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them. You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod. Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar. We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog ([https://laminar.sh/blog](https://laminar.sh/blog)) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction. Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable ([https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr](https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr)). We make money from the managed cloud. We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure? [help](https://news.ycombinator.com/formatdoc) [nucleus777](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=nucleus777)[2 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50158890) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029#50159087)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Interesting. Most of the failures I've seen aren't the agent doing something obviously daft, it's a tool call that returns fine but the result shouldn't be trusted. Stale cached data, or a web page or file with text in it that's basically trying to give the agent instructions. Everything after that looks reasonable, it's just built on a bad input. Can flow-1 flag that kind of thing? And how does it tell the difference between the tool giving back something wrong and the agent misreading a result that was actually fine? From the trace alone those look pretty similar to me. We got examples of traces and errors we caught in them there [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50158910&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154029%2350158910) [scottfalconer](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=scottfalconer)[2 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50159087) | [prev](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029#50158890) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029#50155995)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) We ran into an interesting side effect of agent performance that we needed to explain in our results to our executive team. In our case we were rolling out an AI support agent that could help resolve customer problems. At the start we had calculated the total time and human cost per support ticket going back a few years. After a few months of running the AI agent, we found that both our time and cost per ticket had increased - but then digging in, the issue was that our overall cost and time had decreased and it was just that the more complicated issues the agent wasn't able to answer were the ones now going to the humans, skewing our per ticket cost up. So in this case it's not that it was a different failure, it was that a signal that seemed to indicate failure was actually a signal of success. The net result then is the ones left for the humans are the harder ones. We’ve also heard from other companies that as the first line paper cut questions get answered, customer adoption increases - which further increases the “hard” support questions. Lesson learned for me on that one that was rolling out a support agent led to both a better experience for our customers and an increased need for talented human engineers. [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50159289&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154029%2350159289) [dmos62](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=dmos62)[6 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50155995) | [prev](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029#50159087) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029#50154663)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) How do you reuse traces as benchmarks (eval datasets)? Is it about being able to synthesise an agent session from the trace, and having another agent watch the first agent's behavior? Having trouble wrapping my mind around all the little details. Edit: I initially asked also about general tips for observing agents, but later, noticing that there were no interactions with my comment yet, edited my comment to remove that question, because I felt that it was too broad and would detract from my main question. To my surprise, both were answered by op after my edit; kudos! [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50155995&goto=item%3Fid%3D50154029%2350155995) [dinm](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=dinm)[6 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50156309) | [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029#50155995) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50154029#50154663)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Good questions. Agent observability is based on similar primitives as regular observability (OTEL), but is wildly different. Trace payloads are huge, and errors are much more subtle, they are not increased latency or elevated 500 response rate. We recommend tracing everything in detail, and reading a few traces manually at the beginning while you iterate. At scale, the answer is almost always use another LLM look at your traces, which is what this post is all about. Evals are critical. I really recommend adopting the Anthropic's capability / regression eval model [1]. We also deeply believe that agent evals should be end-to-end, and as high-level as possible. This again often involves a quality LLM-as-a-judge, tuned on a set of manually labelled data. With this idea in mind (to answer your question), we think that, for eval datasets, the most crucial bit is to be able to store input of what your agent was asked about in production. Collect a certain distribution of inputs for happy and unhappy cases, and then run evals on those inputs. That's why Laminar went great lengths to help our users automatically get actual inputs their users send to their agents [2]. Title: Agentic Monitoring

URL Source: https://benjamincongdon.me/blog/2026/10/19/Agentic-Monitoring/

Published Time: 2026-10-19T06:00:00-07:00

Markdown Content:
A [recent Anthropic blog post](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control) contained a short paragraph, not at all the point of the post, which has been buzzing around my brain since I read it:

> A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison.

This is _so obviously_ the path forward for software systems operations. I’ve been thinking about monitoring with agents for the past few weeks, and this paragraph crystallized some of those thoughts.

Modern software systems, like the LLMs that write them, are becoming more “grown” than “designed”. Yes, human engineers often still give the high-level design and shape to the system, and yes, software systems (for now) are much more interpretable than LLMs – since you can just sit down and read the code, if you are so inclined. However, with the volume of code being written and shipped increasing exponentially, the amount of actual eyes-on-code knowledge that any human operator of a system has is decreasing.

Systems monitoring was never _easy_. There is a whole industry of observability SaaS companies – [Sentry](https://sentry.io/), [Datadog](https://www.datadoghq.com/), [Splunk](https://www.splunk.com/), [Honeycomb](https://www.honeycomb.io/), to name a few. Observability is expensive.[1](https://benjamincongdon.me/blog/2026/10/19/Agentic-Monitoring/#fn:1) Doing it well requires a specialized human skill set and relies on building experience operating real systems at scale. One can really only develop these skills by working in industry. This is a domain that takes years to train junior engineers on.

As with seemingly everything in the software industry in 2026, system monitoring is poised for a step change due to agents. I… am surprised I have not seen more people write about this, especially in the current milieu of “agent frenzy”. It’s right there in front of us all, and it _works_. There have been a bunch of startups trying to do the “AI SRE”, but very little writing from practitioners.

But you don’t really need a full “AI SRE” to improve operational excellence, nor do you need a built-out SaaS product to do so. As of the Opus 5.5 / Astra class of models, with a bit of care, it’s entirely possible to make a good agent-driven monitoring system that “just works”.

### Case study: change-point monitoring

I’ll ground this discussion in a problem that is near to my heart: production monitoring of change points, like binary releases and [config pushes](https://benjamincongdon.me/blog/2026/03/12/Feature-Flagging-at-Databricks/). The idea is that you want to do specialized, intensive monitoring around critical points of change to a system; these change points are more likely to trigger a regression, and thus if you monitor these events closely, you can limit its impact. To quote the clichéd line from the Google SRE book, “~70% of outages are due to changes in a live system”.

This is a [wicked problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wicked_problem). I’ve been working on it in some form since 2023, and it’s been hard to get traction on. From talking with folks across the industry, I’ve learned there are ways to do change-point monitoring “well”, but these methods largely still rely on humans to do the right thing (e.g. tagging metrics/alerts diligently, defining precise signals, etc.) and require significant organizational investment.

More specifically, achieving “takeoff” for change-point monitoring as a piece of platform engineering is hard because:

*   Your first instinct may be to target highly motivated users who already have a good ops posture. However, these teams’ rollouts are already mostly safe, and you don’t actually raise the ops waterline much. The thing you’re selling here is _toil reduction_, which is “nice to have” but is not itself a first-order safety improvement. Precision is easier to achieve for highly motivated teams, but this means the change-point system is “competing” on recall and latency with traditional alerts.
*   You can alternatively target the broad population of services. In other words, you go super wide and opt in “all services”, on a chosen subset of universal health metrics. In practice, most of these general health metrics are irreducibly noisy. This noise results in poor precision and alert fatigue.
*   Prior to LLMs, there was a clear precision/latency tradeoff as well. Along this spectrum are: structured logs (precise, slow), metrics (coarse, fast), and alerts (even coarser, recall is pretty bad and precision is pretty bad, but “at least it’s something”).

Shockingly, agents largely “just” solve this problem. Agents are happy to run copious queries, can write per-change queries on the fly, and will scan logs ad nauseam. As a result, you can get both good precision and recall for cheap. In the basic version of this setup, you just need the ability to connect your codebase (e.g. to reason about config consumption) and your observability stack (e.g. to view and monitor the live production state) to the agent.

I’ve spiked a prototype of exactly this: an agent that proposes a monitoring plan based on the service code, a scaffold that executes that plan, and an agent that investigates triggered monitors, with an escalation path to humans. Even in this early prototype, I’ve been able to detect regressions in systems I have _zero_ understanding of with precision and latency that would have been impossible a year ago.

In my iteration on this, I’ve found that a pure agent loop is not the optimal shape for agentic monitors. Rather, a harness that allows the agent to write a spec of how to monitor, along with a deterministic system for running those specs, produces significantly cleaner signals with dramatically lower token usage. To the extent there is “secret sauce” in this pattern, it’s in the noise-reduction heuristics, the prompts that get the agent to write good specs, and a labeled eval set large enough to validate further tweaks.[2](https://benjamincongdon.me/blog/2026/10/19/Agentic-Monitoring/#fn:2)

### Agents are structurally well suited to monitoring

Two mindset shifts need to happen before this pattern can catch on:

1.   Agents actually can do a much better job at monitoring than humans.
2.   Monitoring agents need scaffolding, the same way the rest of the software development lifecycle had to adapt for coding agents. There hasn’t been a “Claude Code moment” for monitoring yet.

Once you make these shifts, monitoring agents have several “unfair advantages” over human operators:

*   Ability to track everything, 24/7. If tokens are cheap, then any regression in a metric you care about and any suspicious log line can be investigated – not just the events that would previously have risen above the “human attention cutline”. Agents don’t need to [“follow the sun”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Follow-the-sun).
*   Ability to fan out and investigate several paths toward resolving a production problem. Agents can parallelize investigations when multiple things go wrong at once, and coordinate quickly. This is already my go-to for incident triage: I just launch a bunch of agents to investigate several potential threads or theorized incident causes. Right now, this is human-driven, but there’s really no reason it couldn’t be agent-initiated in the future. You can elastically scale up a fleet of incident responders.
    *   We’re already seeing that this is becoming critical for security incidents. Teams/fleets/swarms of agents are being used for offensive cyberattacks, and defenders are beginning to build up similar defensive capabilities (e.g. OpenAI’s [Daybreak Blue](https://openai.com/index/expanding-daybreak-as-the-cyber-defense-window-narrows/), Anthropic’s [Project Glasswing](https://www.anthropic.com/glasswing), Google’s [Fairwind](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/)).

*   Ability to respond faster to a problem than can a human. Agents can read code faster than humans. Agents can also query and digest metrics and log signals significantly faster. This speed doesn’t always translate into faster incident detection time; a human with a deep understanding of a system may still be faster at finding the right signal and intuiting the root causes. But to the extent that tacit knowledge can be recorded and made available to an agent, the agent will eventually beat the human on speed.
    *   By extension, for systems where the human operator isn’t deeply experienced, the “time to understanding” is going to be shorter for an agent.

### “A new level of operational excellence is possible.”

**Be more diligent:** You wouldn’t pay a full-time software engineer to look through all the Git commits for a service, pick out things to monitor, and make special short-term fast-trigger alerts just on those changes. However, for a couple cents per million tokens, it’s possible now, and will become an industry standard.

**Continuously improve performance:** Agents can monitor performance, look at heap dumps and stack traces and CPU profiles, and propose optimizations from the patterns they find. Put the proposed improvements behind A/B tests if necessary, and monitor as you would any other change to the service.

In one instance, I observed that a few sessions of Astra/Opus investigation discovered 50% heap savings and 30% latency reduction in a common hot-path library that humans had already spent nontrivial effort to optimize. Once you give a sufficiently powerful LLM a VM and benchmarks to run, the “hill-climbing” ability of current-generation LLMs is remarkable.

**Take action**: Thus far, I’ve mostly been discussing “read-only” monitoring systems. Agents, of course, needn’t be “read-only”. With the right harness and guardrails in place, there’s definitely a future in which agents will be able to take front-line actions to remediate incidents. This could span anything from well-scoped operational tasks like resizing instances or rotating compute pools, to deterministic actions like rolling back a config change or binary, to open-ended tasks like root-causing bugs, proposing fixes, and redeploying on-the-fly. Obviously there is risk the more control you hand-over to the agent, but considering how much agent capabilities expanded over the course of the past 12 months, the amount of write-path work that can be responsibly handed over to agents is bound to increase. The promise of truly self-healing systems is exciting.

**Cost is no longer a limitation.** Luna/Haiku-class models[3](https://benjamincongdon.me/blog/2026/10/19/Agentic-Monitoring/#fn:3) are now competent graph-starers. A moderately large tech company could likely monitor its entire fleet for on the order of $100/day. Startup-scale fleets would be a small fraction of that. Compared to human labor, or even the cost of the infra that runs observability, this is trivial.

**Create a virtuous cycle:** If done well, agentic monitoring creates a positive feedback loop: coding agents allow you to ship more, monitoring agents allow you to support more systems, which in turn frees up human time to direct more things to ship. articles.content:
In the middle of an
especially warm
July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.
The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had
reached 12 feet
in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.
A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail.
In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route. About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors.
Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies
15% of the land
around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.
A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface. But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground.
“That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.”
Researchers Eric Miller (left) and Alison York (right) record thaw depth at the site of the Yankovich Road Fire.
LEIF VAN CISE
This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north. As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost. This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost.
Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada
released more carbon
than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023. As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats. Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon.
Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically. They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control. They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon.
“We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire," says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference."
Woodwell scientist Brendan Rogers (above) has been studying the impact of Arctic-boreal fires on permafrost, as well as what could be done about it.
PHILIP KEITH (PHOTOS), WOODWELL CLIMATE RESEARCH (MAPS)
Woodwell, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the nonprofit Alaska Venture Fund are now partnering on a multimillion-dollar initiative
known as North Fire
to study and raise public awareness about the potential benefits of these interventions,
MIT Technology Review
can report.
The idea is complicated and controversial for a number of reasons. Wildfire is a natural and necessary component of healthy forest ecosystems. Preventing or suppressing fires across huge stretches of largely unmanaged Arctic-boreal forests and tundra would take vast resources. And it’s not yet clear how much of a difference such interventions would make in emissions.
Ultimately, the mere fact that researchers are considering such extreme interventions into natural systems is a grim reflection of the dangers we’ve placed ourselves in by continuing to generate more and more greenhouse-gas emissions each year. Those threats are forcing us to grapple with increasingly difficult questions that involve ever steeper trade-offs: What’s the best way to spend our finite resources and dwindling time to avoid the worst dangers of climate change? And when, if ever, is it okay to put people in possible danger to reduce broader risks to the world?
‘A massive blind spot’
Emissions from forest fires have risen
60% around the world
since 2001—but they’ve nearly tripled across the boreal forests in the far north.
This stretch of the globe is warming as much as four times faster than the rest of the planet, drying out the landscape. In addition, lightning strikes that set off fires have ticked up sharply as warmer air increases the convective energy in the atmosphere, driving the updrafts that trigger thunderstorms.
In that sense, humans have already interceded in these otherwise natural ecosystems by producing the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, subjecting forests to fire patterns well outside healthy historic norms.
“To me, that outweighs the existential dread of ‘Should we or should we not intervene?” says Kate Hayes, an assistant professor at Western Washington University, who is working with Woodwell to study the emissions benefits of fire interventions. “We’ve already intervened, arguably. And so from here, it’s a little bit of a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.”
The permafrost that encircles the northern latitudes, underlying large stretches of Canada, Greenland, Siberia, Scandinavia, and other Arctic nations, stores
around 1.5 trillion tons
of carbon, much of which froze in place millennia ago. The steady global rise in temperature, however, has already shrunk the footprint of Arctic permafrost
by about 12 %
since 1850, with that loss rapidly accelerating during the last 50 years.
By 2100, fire-driven thawing of permafrost could release about the equivalent of nearly 80 billion tons of carbon dioxide, under high warming scenarios. That’s more than half the emissions that fires will release from the direct combustion of vegetation, according to a
January study
. And it would be on top of more than 400 billion additional tons that could be released through thawing from general warming over that period.
Despite its growing contributions to climate change, only a minority of the models that have informed the UN’s major climate reports to date include the gradual loss of permafrost through warming temperatures, and
none incorporate
the abrupt collapse and accelerated thaw that can often occur after fires and heat waves. In light of those phenomena and other powerful and undercounted climate feedback effects, we’re almost certainly underestimating how rapidly the planet will warm up, as scientists warned in
a paper
earlier this year.
These warming-driven emissions are a “massive blind spot,” says Brian Buma, a senior climate scientist at the Environmental Defense Fund and a coauthor of the paper, who is working to develop tools that could help fire agencies decide which fires to prioritize.
As escalating fire and permafrost emissions become significant additional contributors to climate change, some researchers have begun to explore what it might cost to take on the responsibility of preventing them, in much the way we’ve sought to cut the pollution from power plants, vehicles, and factories.
A
2022 paper
in
Science Advances
, led by researchers at Woodwell and the Union of Concerned Scientists, found that making greater efforts to put out boreal fires could be a cost-effective climate solution—comparable to, or even cheaper than, addressing emissions by building wind turbines, solar farms, or carbon-sucking factories.
The Yukon Flats pilot
Those economic findings were instrumental in getting more researchers to take the idea of tackling fire emissions seriously, says Peter Frumhoff, a coauthor of the 2022 paper and now a senior science policy advisor at Woodwell.
For several years now, Woodwell researchers have been in discussions with forest managers, fire agencies, Indigenous communities, and other groups across Alaska to communicate the potential of this approach.
It hasn’t been an easy sell, given the constrained resources and tightly defined mission of the
federal and state agencies
responsible for combating fires in Alaska. The general policy there is to allow fires in remote territories to burn unless they
present a direct danger
to communities.
“Those agencies are tasked with protecting life and property now, and to a lesser extent natural resources,” says Randi Jandt, a fire ecologist at the Alaska Fire Science Consortium. “But they’re not tasked to save the world.”
There was one notable early success, however.
The Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge is an 11-million-acre patchwork of wetlands, forests, and bogs. The foothills sit above a particular type of frozen soil known as yedoma. It’s an especially deep, ice-rich, and carbon-dense form of permafrost, composed of massive wedges of silty, wind-blown sediments frozen during the late Pleistocene, which ended about 11,700 years ago. (It also presented
ideal conditions
for preserving mummified remains of woolly mammoths.)
“It took kind of the last ice age to accumulate,” Hayes says. “So there’s no rapid way to re-accumulate it. We can’t really put it back.”
LEIF VAN CISE
LEIF VAN CISE
LEIF VAN CISE
Members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium hike into areas affected by fire to measure the layers of ash left in the soil on the forest floor.
In 2019, the region suffered a series of devastating fires that burned some
750,000 acres
. After an Alaska Fire Science Consortium meeting at which Woodwell scientists highlighted the possible climate benefits of more aggressive fire suppression, the refuge's then manager, Jimmy Fox, began exploring the possibility of putting out blazes when they threatened that permafrost, whether or not they threatened human habitations.
The early reaction was not encouraging.
“You’re going to have people jumping out of airplanes with parachutes to save frozen woolly mammoths—and maybe dying from that?” he recalls being asked.
But eventually, he persuaded managers at the US Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Fire Service to carry out a pilot project on a 1.6-million-acre section of the Yukon Flats. They agreed to try to put out fires there if they had the resources available and believed they could contain a blaze within 72 hours.
Woodwell and its partners agreed to study how that change affected permafrost loss and fire emissions, in the hope of making the case for similar programs elsewhere.
It wasn’t clear the pilot program would survive after Donald Trump was reelected, particularly once the DOGE initiative retroactively cut the public funding for that research collaboration.
But in February, the federal government formally preserved the program and broadened its rationale to include goals like protecting habitat diversity, water quality, and air quality.
Mapping and modeling
One of Woodwell’s main tasks now is determining when and where fire agencies should step in. C

Title: Timestral: Mistral's First Family of Time-Series Foundation Models

URL Source: https://mistral.ai/news/timestral/

Published Time: 2026-07-15

Markdown Content:
Thinking

Summary

Today, we’re releasing Timestral, our first family of time-series foundation models. Our largest model, at just 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks, GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, outperforming the previous state of the art with only two-thirds of the model parameters.

Timestral delivers probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and supports past-only and known-future covariates. Our family of models sits on the Pareto front of forecasting accuracy versus model size, delivering leading performance at each size. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.

Time series is one of the most common data types in enterprise, from sensor telemetry to observability metrics. Forecasts built on it drive decisions in capacity planning, energy, supply chains, risk and maintenance.

Industrial plants forecast process sensors against the production schedule, catch equipment drift before it fails, and plan capacity and spare parts across thousands of assets. Finance teams forecast flows, volumes, and volatility to inform positions, hedging, and treasury across thousands of accounts.

Classical models such as ARIMA and linear regression remain well-established tools for forecasting time series. These models are usually fitted to a single series and learn only from that series' history.

Deep learning models such as PatchTST add the capacity to learn nonlinear patterns across many related series, but they are still typically trained from scratch on each dataset, so what they learn doesn't carry over to new domains.

Time series foundation models bring the pre-training approach to time series. Trained on a large and diverse corpus, our model learns patterns that transfer across series, forecasting zero-shot on data it has never seen, even in domains where data is scarce.

## Benchmark Results

We evaluated Timestral on the three main public forecasting benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. Among pre-trained, zero-shot models, it ranks first across all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.

_GIFT-Eval, top ten of 83 comparable pretrained and zero-shot entries. Lower is better._

_TIME, top ten of the 35 leaderboard entries. Lower is better on both metrics._

_fev-bench, top ten of the 37 leaderboard entries, by SQL skill score. Higher is better._

## Family of models optimised for every specification

Timestral has been optimised as a family of four models: 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models improve forecast performance, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe. Every size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size: for each model size, no public model forecasts better.

_Score vs model size on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench (shown as 1 − skill score). Lower is better. Our 28M model beats Chronos-2, about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Our 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 with fewer parameters._

Timestral does not need a GPU at inference. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 10 ms with the 5M model and 140 ms with the 209M model. Smaller models trade some accuracy for speed: the 28M model is five times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.

## An industrial example

Consider an industrial plant with thousands of sensors across its equipment. Timestral can improve the forecasts on that data in several ways.

**Multivariate forecasting.** A pump's vibration, temperature and pressure don't move independently. A rise in one often explains or causes a change in another. Timestral models related series jointly, so it can use those dependencies instead of forecasting each sensor in isolation.

**Probabilistic forecasting.** A single predicted value may not show the full picture. Timestral predicts a full set of quantiles, so teams can see how wide the uncertainty is, set alert thresholds that reflect it, and plan maintenance around risk rather than a single number.

**Categorical covariates.** Some covariates take values from a set of categories rather than continuous numbers, such as the day of the week, or a machine's state (running, idle, under maintenance). Encoding these as numbers would impose an order or scale they don't have. Timestral takes them as categorical inputs directly to improve forecasts.

**Known-future covariates.** Some drivers of sensor behaviour are known in advance, such as production schedules, planned shutdowns, weather forecasts. Timestral can condition on them to improve forecast quality, so a scheduled load increase is expected rather than flagged as a surprise.

**From Model to System**

Timestral is a numerical model that can run inside existing monitoring pipelines, or be paired with our language models in multi-modal agentic workflows.

In the plant, that could look like this:

1.   Timestral running continuously on the plant's sensor streams, detecting anomalies as they occur.

2.   When it flags an anomaly on a pump, an agent embeds the signals and compares against embeddings of past sensor data to find similar historical failures.

3.   The agent then starts sub-agents to run a root cause analysis, drawing on context from that plant, such as maintenance records, shift logs and operator notes, equipment manuals, past work orders, and readings from related equipment.

4.   The agent drafts a suggested diagnosis based on the findings, with supporting evidence and possible next steps.

The plant manager gets a diagnosis and a plan backed by the sensor data, rather than just an alert.

## Key technical contributions

Several ideas have been combined to produce these results. Each will be described in detail in the technical report.

1.   **Decoupled Horizon Forecasting.** Causal decoders trained with contiguous patch masking, as in Toto 2.0 and TimesFM-3, mask out the values to be forecast, so they look like missing values and are also lost as context for later forecasts. Our approach, DHF, separates the two: the full history stays in the sequence, and learned forecast tokens read the history before them. Every observed value thus serves as both target and context, true gaps stay flagged as missing, and training horizon lengths and missing-data augmentation can be tuned independently of each other.

2.   **Covariate-aware attention.** Each input series is assigned a role: target variate, past-only covariate or known-future covariate. Known-future covariates are visible across the whole window while targets stay causal, and information flows only from covariates to targets. Timestral can therefore use a holiday calendar or a weather forecast without leaking a target's own future into its forecast.

3.   **Synthetic-first data.** The majority of the training data was synthetic. We first generated univariate processes with coherent temporal dynamics, including trends, seasonality and diverse noise patterns. We then used a multivariate synthesizer to construct multivariate series by introducing nonlinear dependencies between these processes.

4.   **Two-stage training.** Timestral is first pre-trained at scale on purely synthetic data with context size 8192, then post-trained on a mix of real and synthetic data with a 4x longer context. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS.

## A model that can be adapted

Public benchmarks measure general performance, but production data can be significantly different in behavior and structure. It may also shift over time as markets change regime, equipment degrades and demand patterns move. The lasting value lies in being able to adapt a model to in-domain data and keep retraining it as the distribution moves.

For organisations that want to go further, Timestral is available through [Mistral Forge](https://mistral.ai/products/forge/), the same training pipeline we use for our language models. It supports:

*   **Zero-shot inference** out of the box.

*   **Architectural extensions**, such as domain-specific covariates.

*   **Fine-tuning on proprietary data**, specialising to a domain while preserving general performance.

*   **Control over the training data**, including adjusting the training mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic data samples to reflect the target domain. Full control over the data ensures that nothing we backtest was seen during pre-training.

The full pipeline can be deployed on our clients’ hardware, including air-gapped environments.

## What’s next

We have published a [GitHub repository](https://github.com/mistralai/timestral) so you can run Timestral on your own data. A technical report with the full results will follow. For more specialised forecasting problems, or to collaborate on research, please reach out to us.

| Parameters | 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M |
| Context length | 32,768 time steps |
| Output | Probabilistic forecasts, 21 quantiles |

[Chicago O'Hare International Airport](https://simpleflying.com/flight-tracker/airports/ord/) (ORD) has uncovered a 50-ton boulder buried approximately 30 feet (9 meters) beneath its airfield, turning an unexpected construction discovery into a public naming contest, according to [CBS News Chicago](https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/voting-contest-name-giant-rock-chicago-ohare-airport/). The rock was found during excavation work for a stormwater management facility connected to the airport’s ambitious ORDNext expansion project. After receiving nearly 3,000 public suggestions, the City of Chicago announced six finalists on October 16, 2026, and opened online voting to decide the boulder’s official name. The winning entry will eventually be displayed alongside the enormous rock in a new [airport](https://simpleflying.com/tag/airport/) exhibit.

Although the discovery has little direct connection to aircraft operations, it offers an unusual glimpse into the work taking place beneath one of the world's busiest airports. [O’Hare is undergoing a major redevelopment](https://simpleflying.com/chicago-ohare-global-terminal-modernization-project/)[to modernize its infrastructure and expand its terminal facilities](https://simpleflying.com/chicago-ohare-global-terminal-modernization-project/), which requires extensive excavation and construction. The boulder was not an anticipated attraction, but its size and unusual discovery have given the project a distinctly Chicago twist. Instead of removing it from the construction site, airport officials decided to invite the public to help give the geological curiosity a permanent identity.

## Six Names Compete For O’Hare’s Biggest Rock

Credit:
Chicago O'Hare International Airport, Simple Flying

Chicago's Department of Aviation discovered the boulder while workers excavated the South Detention Basin, a stormwater management facility being developed as part of the ORDNext terminal expansion program. According to CBS Chicago, the rock measures approximately 11.5 feet (3.5 meters) wide, 8 feet (2.4 meters) deep, and 7.5 feet (2.3 meters) tall. Its estimated weight of 50 tons makes it a substantial obstacle during excavation, although available reports do not indicate it disrupted flight operations. The discovery was made beneath the airfield surface.

The public naming campaign began in September, inviting people to submit their ideas through an online form. Following nearly 3,000 submissions, officials selected six finalists for a public vote, which remains open until 5 p.m. Central Daylight Time on November 2, 2026.

The shortlisted names are:

*    Sweet Stone Chicago
*    No ORDinary Rock
*    Chicago Rocks
*    O'Rock
*    Orchard Rock
*    Da Rock

The public can vote in the city's announced online contest, and the winning name will appear in an airport exhibit.

The contest also builds on the airport's efforts to engage travelers and the wider Chicago community during its ongoing transformation. What began as an ordinary excavation task has become an opportunity to create a small, memorable attraction connected to the redevelopment. According to the initial contest announcement, the winning name will not be carved into the boulder itself; instead, it will accompany it in its planned airport display.

## What Lies Beneath Chicago’s Busiest Airport?

Credit:John McAdorey | Shutterstock

The boulder is made of dolostone, a sedimentary carbonate rock composed primarily of the mineral dolomite, or calcium magnesium carbonate. Geologists identified the material as limestone-related, which can form when magnesium-rich groundwater alters existing limestone deposits. Its presence beneath O’Hare highlights the geological conditions construction teams may encounter during major infrastructure projects. Although the discovery is unusual in its scale, the rock formed naturally over millions of years.

The excavation is part of a much larger effort to improve O’Hare's facilities and accommodate its future needs. ORDNext encompasses the airport's major terminal expansion, which Chicago has described as the largest terminal expansion in its history. The project includes extensive construction and infrastructure work, so excavation extends well beyond the passenger-facing areas where travelers normally see airport development. Stormwater management is particularly important at a large airport, where drainage infrastructure must support extensive paved surfaces and help manage rainfall around runways, taxiways, and other facilities.

The boulder also demonstrates how construction discoveries can become unexpected public-relations opportunities. Airport officials initially referred to it internally as the "O'Hare bean," a playful reference to Chicago's famous Cloud Gate sculpture, commonly known as The Bean. The naming contest takes that informal nickname a step further by letting residents and travelers help shape the airport's history.

O’Hare is a major hub for both United Airlines and [American Airlines](https://simpleflying.com/tag/american-airlines/) and a key gateway for domestic and international travelers. Improvements to its terminals and supporting infrastructure matter not only for Chicago but also for airlines and passengers who [depend on the airport for connections](https://simpleflying.com/chicago-ohare-retook-americas-connectivity-crown-despite-loosing-300-daily-flights/). The discovery of the mega stone has attracted attention to the less visible engineering work supporting the expansion. The planned exhibit will give visitors a tangible reminder of what construction crews found while preparing the airport for its next phase.

For now, the public decides. The winning name is expected to appear alongside the boulder in a new airport exhibit. Whether Chicago ultimately chooses the playful O'Rock, the aviation-themed No ORDinary Rock, or one of the other finalists, the 50-ton discovery has already secured a place in O’Hare's expansion story.
